items.html:
The strongest evidence points to large cluster solves and matrix-free translation work, especially complete gradients. Fields and periodic adjoints remain plausible targets, but their archived timings predate substantial CPU optimizations.

All archive figures below are historical, measured September 19–20 on Ryzen 9950X, four threads, release build at original revision 2470fbe (now 8e93b19). I read JSON directly from the archive without extracting or changing evidence.

Workload Forward Reverse Peak RSS through reverse Implication
Full dense cluster, 256 spheres, lmax=3, D=7680 10.479 s 25.127 s 7316 MiB Largest dense target; cubic solve work and quadratic storage; backward dominates
Full dense cluster, 128 spheres, lmax=3, D=3840 1.538 s 2.986 s 1881 MiB Doubling N increases forward 6.8× and reverse 8.4×
Matrix-free, 1024 spheres, lmax=1, one illumination 2.210 s 2.835 s 47.6 MiB Six forward/adjoint iterations
Matrix-free, 2048 spheres, same parameters 8.781 s 11.294 s 52.8 MiB Six iterations; approximately quadratic cost
Matrix-free, 4096 spheres, same parameters 35.258 s 45.269 s 64.2 MiB Six iterations; matvec work, not increasing iteration counts, drives scaling
Periodic S matrix, 25 spheres, lmax=3 0.521 s 2.396 s 158 MiB Reverse ≈4.6 forward calls
Weighted spherical field, four positions, lmax=3, 131072 samples 2.865 s 4.839 s 87.3 MiB Ample parallel work, but later radial reuse already improved this family substantially
Full spherical field operator, same geometry 2.975 s 5.236 s 2216 MiB Materializing operator costs ~25× memory versus contracted field
Plane operator, 256 modes, 262144 samples 0.331 s 1.113 s 4814 MiB Contrast weighted field: 0.102 s +0.213 s, 265 MiB

Exact archive source: linux-core-performance-20260919.tar.gz. Members have prefix benchmarks/results/linux-core-performance-20260919/ and are:

  • scaling/results/scaling-cluster-n{128,256}-l3-s2048-t4.json
  • illumination/results/illumination-weak-n{1024,2048,4096}-l1-p1-t4.json
  • scaling/results/scaling-array-n25-l3-s2048-t4.json
  • scaling/results/scaling-{field,field-operator}-n4-l3-s131072-t4.json
  • scaling/results/scaling-{plane-field,plane-operator}-n4-l16-s262144-t4.json

Source identity/archive provenance: linux-core-performance.json:17, archive record:454.

My priority order from this evidence:

  1. Avoid solving/materializing unnecessary outputs, then accelerate the remaining large cluster work. Selected LU and weighted fields already demonstrate this strategy. At 512 dipole spheres, the earlier public record has selected LU at 0.381 s versus full T at 0.940 s; matrix-free cuts gradient RSS from 1368 to46 MiB. This is already implemented, so the opportunity is extending its reach and making appropriate user paths use it, rather than claiming it as new. large-problems.md:23

  2. Matrix-free translations: shared/batched RHS, GPU pair kernels, eventually better-than-quadratic algorithms. The archived weak N128 case grows almost exactly linearly with illumination count: 0.02965 s for1, 0.11532 for4, 0.23101 for8, 0.46150 for16, 0.92896 for32, always five iterations per RHS. At32 columns, own selected LU is0.02387 s — 39× faster than matrix-free. This suggests repeated translation arithmetic per RHS; current-source verification is needed. FMM/tree/FFT ideas have larger asymptotic upside, but geometry, conditioning and analytic derivatives make them a research project. Same archive, illumination/results/illumination-weak-n128-l1-p{1,4,8,16,32}-t4.json.

  3. Complete reverse execution, especially dense cluster and periodic problems. Dense N256 spends71% of forward+reverse time in reverse; periodic N25 spends82%. A forward-only GPU success can therefore leave most of an optimization iteration untouched. The older periodic evidence already demonstrated a2× reverse gain from sharing equal-wavenumber Ewald derivatives across polarization, so avoid rediscovering that optimization. evidence.md:221

  4. Batch parallel workloads are good GPU candidates, but reprofile current fields first. September26–30 CPU work already reports field17×/8.6× forward/reverse, EBCM8.4×/5×, cylindrical expansion6.3×/5.4×, cylindrical arrays4.4×/3.2× against an earlier baseline. Those results lack public raw archives, but unequivocally invalidate treating September19 timings as present performance. evidence.md:31

  5. Small dispatch overhead is a narrow, current CPU opportunity. October3 evidence shows added0.3–2.8µs without frameworks and2.0–9.7µs with Advect/JAX/PyTorch/Autograd imported; slab construction19.1→28.8µs. Relevant to many tiny calls; unlikely to dominate large scientific workflows. evidence.md:49

Cautions:

  • Matrix-free N2048/N4096 has no same-size dense reference and uses a dipole, weak-scattering model; do not generalize convergence to high-order resonant clusters. linux-core-performance.json:370
  • Historical16-thread dense scaling is poor, but bounded LU scheduling is already implemented and documented, with2–84× stage-only improvements. It is not an untouched future win. numerics.md:33
  • Fresh setup, factor reuse, recorded forward, reverse, full operator and contracted output are materially different workloads; retain those distinctions.
  • No current timing, GPU run, test, or code change performed. Git/GitHub state unchanged.

Confirmed harness interference, not a sphere-scattering regression. With identical builds, the second worker took2256µs while its idle peer consumed0.12 CPU seconds. Suspending that peer restored38–39µs across six requests. OpenBLAS documents this idle-thread contention. OpenBLAS guidance

Fixed the comparison harness:

  • One fresh worker per tree/case; fully closed before its peer starts.
  • Preserved ABBA ordering and ordinary BLAS settings.
  • Timing batches now actually meet the requested duration; a slow first call previously produced undersized samples.

Verified16 focused tests, lint and formatting. Diagnostic evidence is saved in blas-idle-contention-diagnostic.json. Old results remain untouched; corrected final comparisons await your rerun. No production changes, pushes or PR activity.

items.html:
The source points to overparallelized native matrix products, rather than OpenBLAS, for this particular case.

stack-power-h64 performs two cascades: 14 small dense products. Each64×64 product exceeds the fixed65,536 multiplication-work threshold, so threads.rs:227 gives it the entire32-worker budget. Each matrix occupies only64KiB. Repeated scheduling across32 logical threads—16 physical cores here—can overwhelm useful work.

The other stages do not explain that budget sensitivity:

  • LU factorization and its128-column solve already select one worker at this size. linalg/mod.rs:243
  • Power evaluation uses native matrix-vector products, which explicitly stay sequential.
  • The timed stack/power path does not call NumPy BLAS; slab preparation occurs outside timing.

Your longer same-build control is appropriate. If further attribution is needed, hold affinity and BLAS at one thread while comparing native budgets1/4/32. That isolates native scheduling without changing numerical code.

The broad ratios0.77–1.50 do not yet establish an implementation-specific regression. Retain the failed32-thread row as unresolved pending the control; do not silently waive it.

Read-only inspection only; no edits or timings.
